item.title: 155 mil reproducciones · 1529 reacciones | What happens when we detect an asteroid that could pose a threat to Earth? In early 2025, NASA joined scientists around the world in tracking asteroid 2024 YR4, which had a small chance of impacting Earth in 2032. As the international community studied it more closely, it was ultimately found to pose no threat to Earth — but the asteroid still provided a real-world test of the systems designed to protect our planets. We have the behind-the-scenes story. Tune in and watch Planetary Defenders: This Is Not an Exercise, our newest documentary, now streaming on NASA+. https://go.nasa.gov/46Jm361 | NASA - National Aeronautics and Space Administration

item.title: Studies map microclimates beneath solar panels to help native vegetation thrive in the shadow of renewable energy
item.description: Using solar energy is good for the environment, but look down, and the grass isn't always greener. Solar farms can generate massive amounts of renewable energy, but when they're built in natural areas, they change the growing conditions underneath the panels. That can make it easy for native grasses to be squeezed out by invasive weeds and non-native plants. On top of that, fast-growing turf or other non-native grasses are often used as a less costly, more convenient replacement in reclamation efforts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rotating light pattern reveals laser frequency in a single image
item.description: An international team of physicists has developed a new method for determining the precise color of laser light using an image that rotates as the laser's frequency shifts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scandium's electrons may explain predicted room-temperature superconductivity
item.description: Scientists have confirmed the existence of a predicted room temperature superconductor, while explaining the microscopic mechanism that distinguishes it from a similar one discovered several years ago. The work, published in the journal Physical Review B, offers "a theoretical blueprint for the future design of superior superconductor hydrides" the physicists write. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tokyo suffers the longest streak of rainy days on record
item.description: Tokyo has recorded 34 consecutive days of rain, marking the longest such streak on record, according to Japan's weather agency. Publicado también por: Euronews. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Identical hiring algorithms may create echo chambers that overlook stronger job candidates
item.description: AI tools are increasingly replacing human judgments in some settings. For instance, resume-screening algorithms are often used in hiring, where they may improve efficiency and consistency in decision-making. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study shows California's rodenticide restrictions are working, and flags new rodenticides rising in their place
item.description: New research from the Integral Ecology Research Center (IERC) offers some of the clearest evidence yet that California's efforts to restrict dangerous rodenticides are paying off in the wild, while also flagging a new contaminant that deserves close attention. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: India turns to corals and seagrass to shield against rising seas
item.description: Under a blazing sun, workers crouch on a shrinking island off India's southern coast, threading bright green seagrass shoots onto wooden frames before anchoring them to the ocean floor. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Following a successful inaugural year of ingenuity and career building, NASA ORBIT (Opportunities in Research, Business, Innovation, and Technology) has officially returned for a second season to bring university and college student innovation to the forefront of Earth technology development and deep-space exploration. Registration for the 2026–2027 challenge is open through Monday, Nov. 16, 2026, […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Same plant species, different chemistry: Why chemotype labels matter
item.description: Plants of the same species can differ considerably in their chemical composition, affecting their smell, taste and even toxicity. A new study shows that the term "chemotype" has not been used consistently. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New statistical method can flag hidden anomalies in scientific datasets
item.description: A research team at the University of Vienna, led by pharmaceutical chemist Johannes Kirchmair, has developed a statistical method to identify hidden anomalies in scientific datasets. The method can be applied automatically to large datasets, making it easier for researchers to pinpoint those that need closer scrutiny. The approach improves the quality of data-driven research and supports the development of reliable AI applications. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA ramps up support to get Boeing's astronaut capsule flying after Butch and Suni fiasco
item.description: NASA is throwing extra support and money behind Boeing's troubled astronaut capsule to get it fixed and flying again as soon as possible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: An endangered frog nursery in LA cares for hundreds of tadpoles until they're ready for the wild
item.description: The transition from tadpole to juvenile frog is never easy—legs sprout, tails shrink and lungs develop for a life on land, all while being hunted by fish and other predators. Talk about growing pains. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Feeling like you are losing ground predicts suicidal ideation more than income or age
item.description: New research finds that people are far more likely to report suicidal ideation when they perceive their lives as getting worse relative to their recent past, rather than because of their income, age or health status alone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient bird becomes second Australian species to be named from the Cretaceous period
item.description: A pair of exceptionally rare Cretaceous bird bones found at separate sites near Richmond, Queensland, reveal a previously unknown species—the second formally named Cretaceous bird from Australia. Cretaceous bird fossils are extremely scarce in Australia, with fewer than a dozen isolated bones reported, making these finds especially significant. The research is published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The molecular mechanism that regulates TMEM63B lipid scrambling
item.description: TMEM63B, a mechanosensitive lipid scramblase, has an autoinhibitory domain in its C-terminal tail that helps keep it inactive under resting conditions, researchers from the Institute of Science Tokyo report. Changes to this regulatory region, particularly the Leu776 residue, reverse the inhibitory action and cause continuous lipid scrambling, disrupting normal phospholipid asymmetry. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Half a million older Scots facing fuel insecurity, study finds
item.description: Data from more than 4,000 adults across Scotland showed that fuel, food and financial insecurity are widespread, and more than 1 in 10 adults experience all three simultaneously. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Warming weakens Asian monsoon's reach into the Mediterranean
item.description: The South Asian summer monsoon has long been known to shape the Mediterranean climate thousands of kilometers away as part of a phenomenon known as the "monsoon–desert" mechanism. Through this mechanism, intense monsoon convection during the summer releases large amounts of heat into the atmosphere, triggering large-scale circulation changes that promote sinking air over the Mediterranean. This process suppresses clouds and rainfall and contributes to the Mediterranean region's hot, dry climate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Under the Microscope: NASA-Made Material for Moon Manufacturing
item.description: Photos taken using a microscope reveal the colorful, kaleidoscope-like crystal structure of a new NASA-made material that could be used for manufacturing during future space missions. Developed at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland, the material could be created directly on the Moon or Mars, allowing NASA to pack fewer supplies — saving weight and […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Peeling crust beneath Italy's Apennines may explain why mountains stretch and squeeze
item.description: Extending some 1,200 kilometers (750 miles) along the length of Italy, the Apennine Mountains present a challenging puzzle for geologists. In some places, the mountains are steadily being stretched apart, while in regions just tens of kilometers away, they are squeezing together. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will open a window into the Milky Way
item.description: Look up at the night sky with the naked eye and it may seem like it rarely changes. Yet the universe is in constant flux. Stars drift through space, orbiting the center of the Milky Way as planets orbit them. They rotate, showing spots on their surfaces and sometimes producing violent outbursts that affect planetary atmospheres much like solar storms produce auroras on Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The novel on your nightstand may be doing more for your empathy and cognitive health than you think
item.description: A popular narrative across Instagram Reels, business podcasts and magazine covers is that people who are smart and serious about growth read nonfiction. Nonfiction directly provides factual information and real-world knowledge, whereas fiction, like novels and poetry, is treated as a less practical cousin. Now, a recent study has asked whether fiction really is just entertainment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Diving into an out-of-sync galaxy
item.description: Galaxies are like snowflakes: No two are exactly alike, even the spirals. The Hubble Space Telescope took a close look at the distant spiral NGC 4693 and found intriguing hints about its past. For one thing, this member of the Virgo Cluster seems to have a central region that's rotating out of sync with its spiral arms and bulge. Those arms don't seem to connect to the central region, and the bulge itself seems to extend above the plane of the galaxy. In other words, there seems to be a decoupling between the arms and the bulge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Biologists may have discovered two of the world's loudest birds
item.description: University of Massachusetts Amherst's Jeff Podos and his former graduate student João C.T. Menezes have identified two contenders for the title of world's loudest bird: the bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema. Their findings also help explain why some birds are so much louder than others. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nature-strip gardens boost biodiversity, bugs and social benefits
item.description: University of Melbourne researchers have found that planting native gardens on suburban nature strips can boost urban biodiversity, with insect numbers increasing sevenfold and the number of species approximately doubling. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Perceived motives help explain why some online campaigns fail to mobilize support
item.description: Flinders University researchers have examined the role social media plays in expanding social movements and found that perceptions of online activists' motives can significantly affect others' willingness to participate. The study is published in the journal New Media & Society. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Wearable nanotech could combat nerve agents
item.description: Nanoparticles could someday provide a new way to help soldiers fight back against deadly nerve agents on the front lines. In a new study, Northwestern University scientists developed a nanoparticle-based compound that, when mixed into clothing dyes, could limit the impact of chemicals commonly found in pesticides, insecticides and nerve agents. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Sneakers to Scrubs mentorship program shows data-backed promise
item.description: A new study highlights the promising early impact of Sneakers to Scrubs (S2S), a medical pathways program founded by Black medical students and former athletes to address the severe underrepresentation of Black men in medicine. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Overlooked lakes may be helping to keep the Northern Hemisphere cool
item.description: Lakes may cover only a small fraction of Earth's surface, but new research suggests they play a bigger role in regulating the planet's climate than previously recognized. By reflecting sunlight back into space when covered in snow and ice, lakes in the Northern Hemisphere have a stronger cooling effect than the surrounding land. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New sound catalog reveals who's who in the world of killer whales
item.description: A new open-access catalog of whale calls will help researchers and orca enthusiasts identify distinct killer whale populations, clans and family groups by their vocalizations alone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En 1971, un astronauta llevó 500 semillas hasta la Luna. Medio siglo después son árboles gigantes repartidos por la Tierra
item.description: En 1971, cuando la NASA preparaba el Apollo 14 , alguien decidió aprovechar el viaje para enviar hasta la Luna un cargamento bastante más extraño que cualquier instrumento científico: cientos de semillas de árboles. Viajaron hasta allí, dieron 34 vueltas alrededor de nuestro satélite y regresaron a la Tierra después de sobrevivir incluso a un accidente que hizo pensar que habían quedado destruidas. Más de medio siglo después, aquella diminuta carga se ha convertido en algo enorme. Semillas rumbo a la Luna. La idea nació de una colaboración entre la NASA y el Servicio Forestal de Estados… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
item.description: Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Investigadores crean aeronaves ultraligeras para explorar una región casi desconocida de la Tierra. Su truco: surfear la luz del Sol
item.description: Entre la estratosfera y la termosfera se encuentra una franja en la que termina el alcance de los aviones y globos, pero también donde empieza el dominio de los satélites. Se trata de la mesosfera y, en su parte más alta a unos 70 km, hay una zona inexplorada que se ha apodado con humor científico como ignorosfera. Es extremadamente difícil de estudiar y el motivo es un problema físico. A esa altitud hay tan poco aire que un avión convencional o un globo no pueden mantenerse a flote, pero el aire restante es suficiente para frenar cualquier satélite y hacerlo caer. item.description: China is offering the world’s brightest young scientists generous 15-year research grants for free exploration, as the country accelerates its drive to become a global science powerhouse. Dou Xiankang, director of the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC), the country’s top funder of basic research, told a recent academic forum that the agency was selecting a group of the brightest researchers under 35 for long-term financial backing. item.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
item.description: Image: This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us. MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the… Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Getting AI 'drunk' makes it more likely to break rules, research finds
item.description: A study finds AI models are more likely to answer harmful questions or mishandle confidential information when told to act drunk. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.description: Quienes quieran avanzar en la carrera espacial deben hacer cuanto antes un check muy concreto en su lista de tareas conseguidas: repostar en órbita. Esto es necesario por muchos motivos , ya que es útil para alargar la vida de los satélites, pero también sirve para emprender viajes espaciales mucho más largos, tanto en tiempo como en distancia. Por eso es tan importante el nuevo gran hito de China: el repostaje de un satélite directamente en órbita terrestre alta (casi 36.000 km). item.title: AI identifies Senegal's smallholder crops 84% of the time using limited training data
item.description: Food in Senegal is mostly grown on small-scale, rain-dependent farms, leaving much of the population vulnerable to climate shocks, according to the World Food Programme. However, satellite crop-mapping technologies designed to monitor the impact of climate on farming are largely beyond the reach of the West African country. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 55-million-year-old fossil bird shows how trogons evolved their unusual feet
item.description: A fossil of Daniatrogon kochi, discovered in Denmark, provides insights into the evolution of trogon feet. Researchers found that the trogons' unique foot morphology developed gradually over time. The fossil also shows changes in the shape of their beaks, which were narrower than those of modern species. Additionally, early trogoniforms displayed more varied beak and foot shapes, indicating a diverse ecology. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Earth’s day isn’t exactly 24 hours. The reason may lie deep inside the planet
item.description: Scientists may have solved why the length of Earth’s day changes by a few milliseconds over decades. Subtle shifts in the inner core appear to tug on the mantle, revealing a surprisingly dynamic world thousands of kilometers beneath our feet. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Saving the Siamese crocodile: Cambodia moves to protect one of the world’s last wild populations
item.description: Indigenous communities play crucial role, as ‘genetic bank’ area of wetland offers hope for critically endangered reptile In the 1990s, conservationists in Cambodia feared the Siamese crocodile had disappeared for good. Fishing and hunting had devastated the species throughout the 20th century, leaving populations across its native south-east Asia on the brink of extinction. But in villages dotted among the wetlands of the remote Cardamom mountains, Indigenous Chorng communities still reported seeing them. Passing this knowledge to researchers surveying the area in 2000 led to an official… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: NASA’s Crew-13 could go from Florida to the ISS in under 9 hours
item.description: NASA and SpaceX could launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1, with the Dragon spacecraft reaching orbiting outpost less than nine hours after liftoff. Crew-13 will join Expedition 75 after teams complete a final round of intensive launch-readiness checks. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: This suitcase-sized spacecraft could hear the universe before stars existed
item.description: CosmoCube will use the far side of the Moon as a shield from Earth’s radio noise to search for a faint signal from the universe before the first stars existed. The suitcase-sized satellite could reveal how the cosmic dark ages ended and how dark matter helped build the first galaxies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists expected these Galápagos sea turtles to wander. They stayed put
item.description: Yellow-morph green sea turtles in the Galápagos surprised scientists by staying remarkably close to home instead of making the long journeys typically associated with sea turtles. Satellite tracking showed that none left the marine reserve during the study, revealing just how important the islands’ coastal habitats may be to their survival. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Building Asia's future must embrace the limitations of people and planet
item.description: Japan's population peaked around 2008 and has been steadily declining since. But construction hasn't stopped. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hidden stem cells may be fueling spinal stenosis
item.description: Scientists have discovered a stem cell that appears to serve as a master source for tendon and ligament cells throughout the body. In lumbar spinal stenosis, these cells become unusually active and may drive the ligament overgrowth that squeezes spinal nerves and causes pain, numbness, and difficulty walking. Researchers found that reducing calcium signaling stopped this abnormal growth in mice. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Tracking researchers in Ukraine through war and armed conflict: The limits of free scholarly mobility
item.description: A study based on publication data traces how researchers moved within Ukraine and across borders between 2009 and 2022, with conflict-affected regions losing scholars while others became increasingly important destinations. These shifts were already underway after Russia illegally annexed Crimea and fighting began in the Donbas in 2014, underscoring that scholarly mobility during conflict cannot simply be understood as a matter of free choice. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find new virus behind mysterious tick illness
item.description: Scientists have discovered a new tick-borne virus in China that causes flu-like illness and may account for previously unexplained cases of fever, fatigue, digestive problems, and low platelet counts. Most patients with ALTNV alone recovered, but coinfections with another dangerous tick-borne virus were linked to more serious complications. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: How Bolsonaro's statements destroyed the rainforest
item.description: Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro contributed to deforestation through statements opposing forest conservation, according to an international study led by the University of Bonn. The study found that destruction of the Amazon rainforest accelerated when Bolsonaro and his ministers posted messages opposing forest conservation on Twitter. Brazil's environmental authorities were greatly weakened during Bolsonaro's presidency, but the analysis suggests that even a perceived low risk of punishment was a driver of deforestation. The researchers estimate that the statements contributed to… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: In Japan, anti-foreigner fake news drives far-right gains
item.description: Japan risks being pulled into a spiral of online disinformation about foreign crime that is stoking xenophobia and playing into the hands of the far-right, researchers warn. The trend is reportedly deepening divisions within Japanese society and creating a feedback loop that experts say will be difficult to break. In August, Constella Security Japan, a Tokyo-based cybersecurity firm commissioned by the government to counter online disinformation, hosted a webinar for officials and media on fake... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: When microbial DNA is scarce, new profiling method helps separate genuine signals from contamination
item.description: In acute, life-threatening infections, rapidly characterizing the microorganisms in a patient sample can help guide diagnosis and treatment. Computational methods known as taxonomic profilers can analyze metagenome sequencing data generated from the microorganisms' genomic information and compare it with reference genomes of individual microorganisms. However, taxonomic profilers are still under development and are not yet in common use. Current methods can produce false-positive results or inaccurate abundance estimates. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02776-y Inhibitors of tyrosine kinase enzymes have been a cornerstone in precision cancer treatments. Now, targeted protein degraders could reshape therapeutic options. Fuente: Nature.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03048-5 Researchers in the field are right to focus on biosafety, ethics and the involvement of patient groups and the public. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: How to put people first in cyberspace
item.description: Nature, Published online: 29 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02960-0 Digital technologies increasingly shape everyday life. Computer scientist Francine Berman tells Nature that stronger safeguards are required to protect the public interest. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Fiery end for SpaceX Starship mission
item.description: Elon Musk’s SpaceX's next-generation Starship rocket reached orbit for the first time despite an engine shutdown. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: Dopamine-based nanotubes combine heat, electrical stimulation and antioxidant release for first time
item.description: The research group at the Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia in Pontedera (Pisa), led by Gianni Ciofani, has developed new organic nanoparticles that combine multiple therapeutic functions in a single material for the first time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Party leaders widening Washington's political chasm
item.description: Most of the polarization currently roiling Congress comes from political parties rather than individual politicians, a study co-authored by University of Miami Business School associate professor Chad Kendall finds. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plasma treatment helps reveal how molecular coatings dope silicon
item.description: Controlling dopant concentration near the silicon surface is increasingly important for ultrashallow junctions and nanoscale devices. Mixed monolayer doping (MMLD) offers a surface-chemistry-based approach in which dopant-containing molecules are mixed with nondopant molecules to tune the amount of dopant available at the silicon surface before thermal diffusion. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Two-color glowing molecule could make wind tunnel tests more accurate
item.description: Most sensors can measure only one thing at a time, like a thermometer for temperature or a pressure gauge for pressure. Measuring two properties accurately from the same surface at the same moment usually means using two separate instruments—adding cost and complexity to the process. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Espionage boosted East Germany's economic output by 7.4%
item.description: East Germany's espionage activities in the West boosted the country's economic output by 7.4%. Value added in manufacturing alone increased by 22.3% through industrial espionage, equivalent to 20.2 billion East German marks or approximately 4.1 billion euros at 2020 prices. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hydrogen's distant glow opens new way to investigate dark energy
item.description: The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) has shown for the first time that it can detect the faint glow of hydrogen gas from deep in the universe's past using only its own data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: October’s Night Sky Notes: Spooky Stargazing
item.description: The Ghoul Located within the constellation Perseus lies a star called Algol, also known as ‘Demon Star’ or ‘The Ghoul’. You can spot this star during the autumn months, along with Cassiopeia and Andromeda in the northeastern sky, beginning after 9 PM. In Greek mythology, this star represents the ‘blinking eye’ of the gorgon Medusa. […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: AI news coverage reveals hierarchy of innovators, regulators and overlooked regions
item.description: Analyzing more than 43,000 English-language newspaper articles, a new study reveals a highly stratified narrative about AI in which the news media allocate authority unequally, reinforcing the technology's prominent role in contemporary life. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Assembly pathway reveals how bacteria build protein coils that extend in acid
item.description: The assembly pathway behind refractile-body proteins may have finally been resolved, researchers from Science Tokyo report. Using genetic engineering and several techniques for analyzing protein structure, they investigated how four proteins work together to produce the correct architecture of these complex, pH-responsive protein machines, from the nanoscale to the microscale. The findings could help establish new frameworks for engineering dynamic protein systems as biotechnological tools. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Avian odysseys: Tracking raptor migrations from Europe to Africa
item.description: At the southwest tip of Sweden, the Falsterbo Peninsula stretches into the Baltic Sea, creating a natural bottleneck for hundreds of millions of birds traveling south for the winter each year. Falsterbo is particularly known for raptor migration. One autumn morning, I stood with a group of others by the lighthouse, watching birds gather to cross the open sea—a sight to take your breath away. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European rivers are improving, but not fast enough to meet 2030 goals
item.description: The quality of European rivers has improved in recent years, but not at the pace required to meet the environmental targets set for 2030. This is one of the main conclusions of a study led by researchers María Pachés Giner and Remedios Martínez from the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV), published in Environmental Science and Pollution Research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experimental evidence of altermagnetism in a layered material opens a promising path toward future spintronics
item.description: To build the ultrafast computers of the future, scientists are looking beyond the electrical charge of electrons to another property: their spin. While conventional hardware relies on the movement of charge to process data, tapping into this intrinsic quantum property could enable researchers to reinvent how information travels through a circuit. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Researchers link the rise to immigration politics, economic anxiety and the growing visibility of South Asians in US. Fuente: Al Jazeera English.

item.title: Exposed ends and bends attract DNA-cutting enzymes, live imaging reveals
item.description: Researchers at the Nano Life Science Institute (WPI-NanoLSI) at Kanazawa University have directly visualized how enzymes find and break DNA molecules in real time. Using high-speed atomic force microscopy, the team followed individual enzymes as they moved along DNA and found that they repeatedly returned to vulnerable regions before breaking them apart. The findings reveal how the structure of DNA influences its vulnerability to enzymatic breakdown. The research was led by Richard Wong and his team: Jingge Yang, Yujia Qiu, Keesiang Lim and Toshio Ando. The work is published in Nature… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Subjective and objective difficulty of English texts are related—but not the same
item.description: Evaluating the difficulty of English texts used in educational materials and language assessments is a central concern in English language education. Traditionally, researchers have relied on objective measures of text difficulty based on linguistic features, including characteristics of words and sentences. However, learners can differ substantially in how difficult they perceive the same text to be. To examine the relationship between objective and subjective text difficulty, the researchers investigated the extent to which objective estimates correspond with learners' perceptions. The work… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Meteor hit Oklahoma 100 million years later than previously thought
item.description: Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have rewritten a small part of Oklahoma's geologic history with global implications for ancient life. Below the surface of the small town of Ames, Oklahoma, a meteor impact site spans miles. The crater is buried by sedimentary strata in the subsurface, but it remains an important marker of Oklahoma's ancient past and present-day economy; the Ames impact structure is a major oil and gas producer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Uncovering species–specific chemical sensitivity by focusing on mammalian hormone receptor evolution
item.description: Chemicals affect biological species in different ways, posing a major challenge for assessing environmental chemical risks. However, the mechanisms behind these differences have remained largely unknown. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mapping the 'social network' of proteins in the cell to understand how genes shape living things
item.description: One of biology's fundamental questions is how our genes shape who we are. Adrian Serohijos and Stephen Michnick, professors in the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Medicine at Université de Montréal's Faculty of Medicine, are studying the relationship between genotype and phenotype—that is, how DNA becomes RNA, then protein, and ultimately gives rise to observable characteristics in an individual or any other living organism. "We're trying to unravel the mechanisms of the genome, specifically how the information it encodes is processed inside the cell," Serohijos says. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Changing climate may influence risks from deadly rodent-borne diseases
item.description: Changes in rainfall can trigger increases in rodent populations and subsequent spikes in infection, new research has found, revealing how a changing climate could have consequences for human health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Water-stable catalyst could bring carbon-bond chemistry closer to use in living cells
item.description: Olefin metathesis is one of the most important reactions in organic chemistry for forming carbon–carbon bonds—for example, in the production of pharmaceuticals, plastics and complex natural products. However, previous ruthenium catalysts that enable this reaction have faced a major challenge: They rapidly degrade in aqueous or biological environments, making their use in natural systems such as cells or blood extremely difficult. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient spearheads reveal how Ice Age humans learned the land
item.description: At the end of the last ice age, early humans crisscrossed the Americas following seasons, rivers and game, often with a trusty spear in hand. Nearly 13,000 years later, archaeologists are using those spearheads to study how America's first inhabitants understood risk. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hibernating bacteria can invade hospitals and survive outer space—but their energy budget reveals a weakness
item.description: A spore is a bacterium's survival capsule: dried almost solid and wrapped in protein armor, with its chemical processes shut down. Bacteria enter this state of hibernation when environmental conditions are unfavorable. What's left is close to indestructible: It can survive boiling, desiccation, radiation and the vacuum of space. NASA once bolted Bacillus spores to the outside of a satellite and left them in orbit for nearly six years; the ones shielded from sunlight were able to come back to life upon returning to Earth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Who's really No. 1? Statisticians build a better way to make sense of competing sports rankings
item.description: Who, really, is the best player in baseball? Ask five sports media outlets and you may get five different answers. Rankings can vary dramatically from one source to another, change from year to year and leave out different players altogether, making it difficult to determine where there is genuine consensus and where opinions diverge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why are employees reluctant to disclose AI use to their bosses?
item.description: Countless employees across the country are experimenting with artificial intelligence (AI) to streamline workflows and increase productivity. Yet many are keeping these solutions to themselves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Reid Wiseman, comandante de la misión, tras su regreso a la Tierra: “Estoy ansioso por ver a mis amigos continuar este legado”
item.description: Tras su regreso a la Tierra, Donald Trump le entregó a cada tripulante una medalla Medalla de Honor Espacial del Congreso, durante una ceremonia en el Centro Espacial Jonhson de Houston Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Parking policy masks anti-Muslim discrimination for communities building new mosques
item.description: When the Islamic Society of Santa Barbara welcomed its community to its newly built mosque in 2019, nearly 19 years had passed since it purchased the property. The city's permitting process alone took 10 years. The project faced delays during 16 public hearings, at which residents of the suburban town of Goleta raised concerns, particularly about where worshippers would park their cars. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Invasive marine species set to take advantage of rising seas
item.description: More than two-thirds of newly flooded coastlines worldwide could become suitable habitat for 122 non-native marine species—including Chinese mitten crabs, Pacific oysters and Asian tiger shrimp—by the middle and end of this century. The research, published in Nature Ecology & Evolution, identifies coastal regions at heightened risk, including the eastern United States, the Gulf of Mexico, coastlines bordering the North Sea, southeastern China and northern Australia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: More damaged trees mean fewer ecosystem benefits for low-income residents
item.description: Maya Mangala-Munuma '25 first noticed it in her hometown of Grand Rapids, Michigan. When she walked from an affluent neighborhood to a more impoverished one, it wasn't just the houses and demographics that changed. The trees did, too. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: To find a host cricket, this parasitic fly listens to more than the beat
item.description: A pregnant female Ormia ochracea fly has a challenging problem to solve. She must listen for the song of a male cricket, locate him in the dark and use him as a host for her developing offspring. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Megacohete Starship de SpaceX alcanza órbita terrestre por primera vez
item.description: 🚀 SpaceX lanzó este 28 de septiembre su gigantesco cohete Starship a órbita por primera vez, con el objetivo de completar seis vueltas a la Tierra para demostrar que está listo para el programa lunar Artemis de la NASA. Fuente: France 24 - Español.
item.dc:creator: FRANCE24

item.title: Coast redwoods slow their 'breathing' and 'eating' when temperatures spike
item.description: California's iconic coast redwoods are used to growing in cool, coastal areas where the average temperature is around 59 degrees F (15 degrees Celsius). But as average yearly temperatures rise and heat waves push temperatures above 100 degrees F (38 degrees Celsius), the trees are responding by slowing the very process that nourishes them, according to a study from the University of California, Davis. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Road testing: Research team studies potholes in quest for better asphalt sustainability
item.description: A Missouri S&T research team is studying asphalt binders, the materials that hold road materials together, to better understand how they perform and help improve the durability of Missouri's roads. Because roads are constantly exposed to sunlight, changing weather and the stress of daily traffic, these binders can break down over time, making reliable testing essential. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New tool tracks a hidden protein involved in viral infection and cell cleanup
item.description: Viruses such as influenza A and dengue can hijack a cellular system that helps manage protein aggregates. Previous work by FMI emeritus group leader Patrick Matthias and his team showed that a small protein called ubiquitin plays an important role in this process. Fuente: Phys.org.
